blocks.x: It ought to be on now. We may have to move that up a little bit. A little bit for you. I'll take the speaker off. Okay, that seems to be on now. Now, you might tell who you are, Mr. Elgore, and your birth date. It's the thing we'd like to know. You don't mind telling how old you are?
No, I don't mind that at all.
I'm rather proud of that.
I was born on June the 13th, 1879, in the city of New Orleans.
Now, what is your full name?
My full name is Charles Anthony Elgore.
Had your family been musical?
No. I happened to be the only one who was struck by that particular bee.
When did you start in music? What was the first instrument you started on?

My first instrument was violin, which was my major. I started on that when I was six. And I started with a French teacher who was assistant conductor of the French opera in New Orleans. What was his name? By the name of Francois Kakel. That's K-E-R-K-E-L. I studied with him six years.
What was the very first music you ever remember hearing? Can you remember?
Was it the opera maybe?
Or the street fans?
Mostly opera because my father and mother were both opera fans. And we had the New Orleans French opera, which was not very far from where I was born.
Where were you born, by the way? In New Orleans. I mean, what part of the city, downtown?
In Frenchtown. About what street? And on Burgundy Street.
Oh, yeah.

Oh, at least a couple of times a week, they would always take me to the opera. And of course, having been a student of the conductor, I became all the more interested in the opera because of him and through him. And he made it possible for me to even attend many of the opera rehearsals where I could hear the thing in action. And the more I heard it, the more I fell in love with it. And I think that has much to do with my knowledge of classical music now.
Yes, you think so.
And I delve in that particular phase of music mostly during my younger days up until the time I began to stir the planet with Louis Thiel.
That was the...
That was one of the Thiel brothers from Mexico. The Thiel, yes.
Because later it was the Lorenzo Jr.
Yeah, that's Lorenzo's brother. And at that time, then after I took up the planet, then I began to go in for the popular side of it.
Well, could you tell me while you mention the Thiel so we don't forget it, that they came from Mexico?
Yeah, they originally they were from Mexico, both of the brothers. But they migrated to New Orleans, oh I suppose when they were about in their thirties.
They were about thirty years old.

Because Louis, Louis was better known than Lorenzo. Lorenzo, the older brother, he went in mostly for teaching. If you look back and could compare the playing of all of our old fine planet players such as George Baquet, Charlie McCurdy, there's a boy who died here, Jimmy Noon.
Oh, yes, Jimmy Noon.
And...
Homer Simeon studied from the young Thiel, too.

You find all of those boys are a product of those Thiel brothers. Albert Nicholas. And you find... Albert Nicholas. Barnaby Godd. Barnaby Godd, all of that. All of those boys are of that same school. If you compare their style, you find that they all follow pretty much in that same pattern of technique, which is different from the average planet player that you hear these days.
They're all dead now, that's why I'm asking you. I don't like to bother with a lot of questions.
You mean the T.O.'s? The T.O.'s. Oh, yes. Even the sons. Yes.
So you're one of the few people that can remember them and about... Yeah.
I'll tell you another boy who's a product of that school, too, Buster Bailey. Oh, yes. Yeah.
You say Lorenzo Senior is the one that taught...

Lorenzo did more teaching than... Louie. And Louie, during his younger days, did a lot of traveling. You see, in the old days, we had minstrel troops. And we had... Companies that traveled the country, just like the show that we have now. And they carried their own orchestras and band. And Louie went in for that type of thing for a number of years. But Lorenzo always stayed right in New Orleans. He never did much traveling.
I noticed you say Lorenzo T.O. came with the band Roma.
The band Roma from Mexico.
There was one big band that came up, the Mexican band for the Cotton Exposition in 1885. You don't happen to be... I know you were young.
No, no. I remember that. Yes, I remember that very well. But I don't think, at that time, either one of those T.O.'s were with the outfit. No.
They were already in New Orleans. Oh, there.
Oh, sure. They were already stationed in New Orleans. Before 1885.
Because there was a famous national Mexican band. I have some of the sheet music with a picture of it.
Yeah.
I think Over the Waves was their theme song. They introduced that to New Orleans. They have the picture on the sheet music. It's quite a big band. Oh, yes.

It was a huge thing. It was really a symphonic band. Yes. Because they had cello, bass violins, and all that sort of stuff. Oh, as soon as you see everything in them. Uh-huh. All the things that you find in a regular band, plus the strings. Yes. And the only band that I have heard that compared with that outfit was the God Republic from France.
Oh, really?

When they came here during World War I. We were then playing at the pier. And we didn't play the Sunday afternoon that they were to give the concert, because they used the same stage and auditorium where we were. But having been employed there, we were permitted to stay and listen to the concert. One of the most wonderful experiences I've ever had and shall never forget.

Do you remember any other real early music when you were abroad? When you were a boy, did they have any of the street parades? You know, they have now a lot of the parades. They even use them for funerals and- Oh, gosh, yes.
Yes, sure.
They had the brass bands when you were a boy. Uh-huh.

You know, because I had a taste of that myself after I began running around the country. That was one of my first trips. I went away with an outfit that was organized in St. Louis. And, uh, we traveled around the country for a while and had the misfortune of being stranded. And from there, we- I lined up with, uh, a very famous trumpet player we had by the- who was, at that time, with the Four Point Ring Brothers Circus. His name was P.G. Lowry.
Oh, yes. I heard-

Very, very, very famous trumpet. Well, he was the bandmaster and he heard me play and asked me if I would take the orchestra. And we left St. Louis with that outfit and went to New York, the old Madison Square Garden. And, uh, we rehearsed there for a couple of weeks before we went on the road. And then we went on the road and I stayed out with that outfit, oh, about two years. Then went back to New Orleans, stayed in New Orleans, and of course the old man got after me for about- but running around the country. And I stayed home for a while, but the bug had stuck me. So I had an opportunity to leave and I left and came to Chicago.
I wondered what type of music you heard in the churches. Which church did you belong to? Were you Protestant or a Catholic?
No, no, no. I'm a Catholic. I've always been a Catholic.
Unusual music in the Catholic Church, I guess, has never changed as far as I feel. Unusual music in the Catholic Church, I guess, is that you left New Orleans at what date then?
I left there about, uh, uh, uh, uh, the first part of November, 1902.
You were about 23 years old then.

I was just about, yes, just about 23. When I came here, uh, this local, 208, had just been given a charter. That- the July of that year. Mm-hmm. And, uh, this picture you see up there- Oh, yeah. Is a picture of all of the presidents. The man in the upper left-hand corner was the first president. His name was Alexander Armand, originated from New Orleans himself.
Oh, yeah.
And I became a member here under his administration and have been ever since. These are all the presidents we've had up to the present, Mr. Gray, you see in the center there.
That's the still president.

Mm-hmm. Now, Smith, Smith is gone. Uh, both of the Smiths are gone. The upper one, Ed Smith, and George Smith is gone. The one at the bottom there, Verona Biggs, he's gone. And Swan, up to the right-hand corner, he's gone. Is the Mr. Swift still around? Now, uh, Stewart is still here. Uh, Swift is still here. Dr. Giles is still here, and Mr. Gray.
Mm-hmm.
But all of these- the other persons practically retired from the music game.
You were almost a charter member of the union here.
Well, uh, I came immediately after they got that charter, so I couldn't say that I was a charter member. No, almost. Because- but I was among the first members during the organizations. Yeah.
Uh, how long have you been an officer of the union? Oh, my dear. Ever since I can remember, but that's not so long.

Yes, I've been an officer most of the time. Even from the very first time I came here. In some capacity, but I've been vice president, I guess, about 20 years now. Maybe longer. I have never had any desire for the presidency, because I never felt I wanted to give up my music activities. Which I would have to do if I was at the head of the organization. As it is, I stay in the background as its vice president, and I- I can still function as a musician.
That's wonderful. I think that you have that interest in music, because a lot of people that have been in the business that long may-

No, and I still- and I still do it, because I am now- I have a concert orchestra that's working on the Music Performance Trust Fund, and we give free concerts around schools and hospitals. And I'm getting a tremendous kick out of that work.
That's wonderful.
It keeps me young.

I wondered about the- I know a lot of your activity has been in the concert field we have here, this paper. May we keep this copy, by the way? Mm-hmm. So we'll have that for our files, too, which will also state your education and experience. The Nelson Academy, we might go through a few points there.
That was my first school.
Now, where was that located? I don't remember-
That's in your lane.
About where, about what part of town?
That's right next door to where I was born. Oh, right down? Mm-hmm. It was a private institution. Mm-hmm. Yeah.
I didn't know about it.
Yeah, it was a private institution. And the Southern University- See, my father at that time didn't believe in sending us to public schools. My brother and I both finished there.
Well, today even, they say about half of the students in New Orleans go to Catholic schools. Most of them, yeah.
That's more of them. Yeah, see, and especially in that south, in that French section. Yeah. Very few of the kids there went to public schools.
The Southern University-
That's now merged with the New Orleans, and now they're in Baton Rouge.
And the same, same art you said. Yeah. And then the other was, when you came to Chicago, we have the Marquette up in Millenburg.

Well, I had, I had two years at Marquette where I had a course in public school music. And then I stood at Kimball Hall with Professor Manley, and I took my teacher's course on violin. Yeah. And I had a course of philosophy with Dr. Balduff at the Central YMCA College. Yes.
Now this is a conducting course under Lorenzo Teo.

Yes, that's, we had in those days an organization known as the Club Lyri. That was composed of a symphonic orchestra. People who played just for the love of music. It was a non-profit organization. Their sole purpose was to sponsor talented young people. We used to give two concerts a year, and whenever we found a talented person, we would sponsor them. We sent, I remember we sent one boy to Europe, pianist. And, I don't know, we've never found out what really happened. He died the week that he was to graduate, after spending almost four years in Europe. Then we sent a young violinist there by the name of Edmund Dede. And he never came back to America until he was an old man. And he died of a cancer.
mouth. But that was organization, it's through that organization I got my first training is conducting under Louie Teo. Is it Louie or Lorenzo? Louie. Louie. Yes.
Did he have regular classes at that time for it, or just take you as a private student?
You mean... Conducting. Oh yes, he did his private work, but this was something that he was interested in, and we used to meet once every week.
Who conducted the orchestra, the lyre? This one, the orchestra I'm speaking of?

Louie. Louie Teo. He was the conductor? Oh yeah, Louie Teo. He was the conductor. Yeah. At that time, I sort of... And when he found out that I was interested in that, then he used to let me take some of the smaller things that he felt I could handle. Do you remember? Louie Teo. And I became deeply interested in that phase of it, then I thought I'd study.
Do you remember who else played in the orchestra, the other clarinetists?
Louie Teo. Well, his brother was Lorenzo. Lorenzo was one of them. I don't remember the others.
Do you remember Alphonse Piku ever played? Who? Alphonse Piku.

Oh no, you see, those boys didn't go in for that type of... They had enough training on their instrument, but they didn't go in for that classical side. From the very beginning, they went into the dance field.

Yeah, and they stayed in that dance field. I had thought that Piku did some classical music too. I think somebody told me. We haven't interviewed him very much so far. We did have one interview with him.
He was qualified and capable of playing it if he wanted to, but he was more interested in the popular thing. Because as you well remember, at that time, the Dixonite music was just a thing.
Yes, yes. Of course, that's our main study is going to be in that type of music. Yeah. We're glad to get all of the classical background because all of that helped.
Oh my gosh, yes. It had much to do because until you know your instrument, such as those boys do, you can't be very successful in that Dixonite music because it calls for a lot of technique.
Most of them actually can read too. Oh yeah, sure. Oh yeah, sure.
Now, when you hear this outfit that's at the preview at Fran Jackson, you'll see just what I'm referring to. Every man in there is very thorough musician.

Of course, I've heard a lot of those groups too in the last 20, 30 years and so. But when you first came to Chicago, was there any of that type of music here? Is that what you call the Dixieland type? Or did it compare at all?

Oh yes, the original Dixieland outfit had been here. That was the outfit. The first outfit that came from Chicago and played here before the colored Dixieland outfit came here. That was Bill Johnson's outfit.
Bill Johnson.
Now, Bill Johnson's outfit was the first colored Dixieland outfit. I can recall who came here. And they played at 8th Street Theater with Trixie Freganza.
Do you remember about what year that was? I know it's hard to think about exactly the year, but if you can remember about when, in relation maybe to the First World War. Was it before that?
That was around, I would say, in the vicinity of the 15, 1950.
Around 1915.

Uh-huh. Just a little before the war. Because just about that time, I went, I was playing at the Washington Theater here, 31st and State. And I sent for Emmanuel Perez, Lorenzo Teal, Louis Cottrell, and I brought an outfit here to work for Mike Fritzel. Yes. At that time, Mike Fritzel had a place on Madison and Paulina. Was that the Ansonia? The Ansonia, that's right. And I put them in the Ansonia for Mike. And I had intended, as the orchestra developed, I had intended to take the move over with me. But they were doing so very well at the Ansonia, and Mike was so very pleased with them that they decided to stay there.
Excuse me for interrupting your train of thought, but is Mike Fritzel still here, you think? No, Mike died.
He's dead. Yes. Uh-huh. He, you know, he had this restaurant here at Van State and Lake. About three years ago. Yes, State and Lake.
About four years ago, I remember seeing us later.
Yeah, the place is still there and it's still called Mike. But he was living then, wasn't he? Most people, yeah, most people still call it Mike Fritzel's place.

Yeah, I was going to say, maybe we could interview him too while I'm trying to get on the story, but you know, I didn't know he was dead. Well, what kind of music did the Chicago musicians play? I'm not trying to ask you to run down the music or anything of that kind. I mean, the New Orleans type, you know, was quite different, but I mean, did it compare? Is it good dance music or is it a different type or?
Well, it's, that is, if you want to compare it in the Dixieland field, then it is different. It is different.

I was just trying to put you on the spot because I know you have friends from New Orleans and friends here too. But I don't mind that. Of course, in those days, most of those people aren't playing anymore anyway. I wondered if you could compare what types of musicians here.

Because they don't match up. They don't match up with those boys. They don't match up with those boys. And I'm not afraid to say it because they have not developed themselves musically. See, you take the young fella today after he's had a few lessons and he can run a few scales and he play a few, what they call riffs, then he stops right there. See? And he gets in what they call a combo and that's as far as he goes. Half of the time you hear him play, you don't know what he's playing.
That's what I think.
And of course, people are accepting it and they tell you, well, it pays, yes, it pays, but where are you getting?
The New Orleans fellas, you felt, had higher musicianship, higher quality training.

Oh, I'm not afraid to say that, by all means. Do you think they're in college? Oh, there are, and there are a number, of course. Now there is an evolution that's taking place now that I'm very happy over. That among the younger fellas who are in college now, you'd be surprised at the number of young people who are going in for the serious side of music. And they are meeting with great success and now that the field is broadening and that this prejudice is dying out, there are many, many openings that they are getting into now that are here to fall. They didn't get a chance to enjoy. Now we have one man who's going in, one of our boys, who's going in Grand Park Symphony next month. What instrument? What instrument? He's, oh, Shello. Shello. A man by the name of Donald White. He is now with the Cleveland Symphony, has been with the Cleveland Symphony this his second year. We have another chap from Chicago here, bass, violinist, Richard Davis. He took the audition for the St. Louis Symphony. He was offered the chair, but he refused it because he's with Sarah Vaughan, where he makes triple the salary that the symphony pays. But the opening is there for him anytime that he wants it. What is his name again? Richard Davis. Richard Davis. Mm-hmm. He's in, he's in Sweden now with Sarah Vaughan. I had a card for him the other day.
Is he a member of this local here?
Yes, yes, born in Chicago.
Born in Chicago.
He's a product of the Civic Symphony. Where? He stood it under Fosbender. That's the first bass player of the regular Chicago Symphony.
So you still play violin, you say, right?
Well, I play a little, not so much now because I've lost the hearing in my right ear. And I can't stand the vibration of these strings now, so I have to practically give up playing.
What kind of violin did you have, by the way? I'm just wondering being a violinist.

Well, I had that violin made by an old man, an old German here whom I met, oh, I guess 25 years ago. Glody. He, he was an old violin maker from Germany. And, and at that time I was doing a lot of teaching and I guess I sold about a half dozen violins which he made. And I still have the same one he made for me. You liked it then? Oh, yes, yes.
I was wondering too now about your orchestra that you had here. Remember those Vocalion and Brunswick records called Elgar's Peel Orchestra?

Well, I, I never was happy about those records and they, they didn't go very far. Uh, because in the first place the day we were calling to record those numbers. Here was 15 piece orchestra and about three sheets of music. Well, you can imagine what kind of recording that could make. And then too, it was the old fashioned recording where you had the horns hanging from the ceiling. And it wasn't at all satisfactory.
I was thinking, was one of the titles called Nightmare or something?
Well, one was Nightmare and...
I guess it wasn't a nightmare to you then.
I forget the other two, but they never did get very far with those.
I haven't heard those for several years now because I hardly ever play 78 records, but I did pick those up years ago. Who were some of the outstanding musicians in that orchestra at that time?
Well, we had Donald Howard, clarinet and violin. Joe Sutler on trumpet. We had Will, so memory doesn't function too much.
Second trumpet.
I remember Harry Swift was on trombone.
The piano player that was...
The pianist at that time was Logan Thomas.
And Darnell Howard played...
Darnell Howard was playing clarinet sax and... That would be clarinet sax and violin.
Richard Curry was on drum.
Now he's with Franz Jackson's outfit now at the preview.
We might go through these pictures if these aren't very good prints. This is the band. This is the band. Now this is...
This boy was the pianist at that time. Is that... Now this is Joe Sutler.
Is this Junie Cobb? No, no, no, no.
Oh, that isn't him.
No, no.
That's Logan Thomas.
I showed this to Baby Dogs earlier this evening and he said it was... No, that's Logan Thomas.
And this is Omar Simeon. He's with Webley de Paris now in New York.
On the other side.
Yeah. And this is Harry Beasley. On drums.
And Simeon is in the middle then of the three sax players.
Yes, uh-huh. And this is Joe Sutler, the trumpet player. Yes, so that's... And this is old Will Washington. And he's passed on.
That's what Baby thought too.
Yes, he's passed on. So has this boy.
Let's see, Sutler, I'll make just for the record here, is on the left. The trumpet player on the left facing the... Yeah, uh-huh.
And this is Bill Buford. On tuba? One of the most marvelous tuba players I've ever heard.
Oh yes, he's been on other records too. The trombonist?
Strange, his name was Henry Strange. Uh-huh. I don't know whatever became of him after he left Chicago.
Is this that same violin you were telling about? That's that same violin.
That's that same violin. That's that same violin.
Oh, yeah. And the other sax player, did you tell me his name right next to you?
Uh, I can't think of that chap's name.
It's been so long. That's all right, we have the others placed. Now this is a bigger band here and it's a hard picture to see.
Now this is Simeon again.
Yes, I know I got that from Mrs. Simeon.

And this is Ernest Smith. He just died here about three months ago. He was living in Cleveland. This is the same banjo player, Washington. This is the same pianist, the same drummer. This is Joe Suttler. In fact, this is the same unit. This is the same unit.
The same unit. The same unit.
All in a smaller picture. I see.
Was this picture taken at Milwaukee too, I believe it's...
Yeah, that was taken at the... Wisconsin Roof Garden. Wisconsin Roof Garden.
That's the way the band stand looked. That's right. That was up on top of the hotel? Yeah. Was it up there? How long were you up there in Milwaukee about?

Well, the first time when we opened the roof garden, we stayed there two years. And I came back here and worked 18 months at the Stratford Hotel. Then went back and stayed another 18 months at the roof garden and then left there and opened up the new Eagles Ballroom. At that time they used to call it Grand Avenue.
Yes.
Well, we opened that ballroom when it was first built. We stayed there two years. Then when we left there, we came here to open up the Savoy.
Oh, yes. That's right. I've heard about the band there too.
About seventh
Many of these same musicians were in the band, were they at the Savoy?
When we came at the Savoy?
Were they or had they?
Most of them.
Do you remember many of the people from New Orleans that you worked with? I know Baby Dodd said he worked a few nights at least in that band. I think Zutty Singleton had too.
Zutty, I tried to get low at that time, but Lowey just about that time had made up his mind to organize his own band. And I had Freddie Keppert.
Oh, Freddie Keppert.
Yes, I had Freddie Keppert.
Well, I think of it. I don't like the... Well, the motorists have this on the tape either. But do you know if Freddie Keppert's widow would be living here anymore?
I don't know. I've never... I've never... I never see her, never hear anything more of her since she's passing.
I know his brother, Louie Keppert, in New Orleans.
Is that so?

I've already interviewed him. He's a wonderful man. He plays guitar. He's really a fine fellow. And we enjoy seeing him. I was going to ask again about... I know you never did much in the dance music in your early days, but do you remember much about the dance music that you heard in New Orleans? Any of the big balls or even carnival balls or other kind of... Oh, gosh, yes.

Yes, because I played... I played with a... Even while I was studying classic side, I played with an orchestra there named Fields and Planchet. And that was the popular combination for most of the club dancers. And I did quite a bit of playing with them.
Do you remember any of the clubs that you played for, the halls?

Well, I remember... Well, there's one hall there, which was the popular hall for club dancers. It was called... It was French name, Frans Amis. Yes. And I can't remember the other hall, but there were two halls that were the popular halls for club dancers. We did. Perseverance.
We did. Oh. Oh. Good. That's working all right. You can get about a half hour on each side of that.
Can you imagine that?

Most of the machines now are being made this way to... Oh. Turn it over and the car is only on half of the tape and the upper half will be taken up. Anything else about the dance music? What kind of bands? They always had a violin, did they in those days, I understand?
Well, I... In the later years, I took up saxophone.
I mean, the New Orleans bands, did they always use a violin? The violin and the dance bands?
No. No. No. Not as much as the clarinet because... Having... More or less on the Dixon Land idea, there was always that clarinet.
That's what I always thought the violin didn't fit in so well. Yes. Yes.
They still tell me sometimes... But we did have orchestras. Oh, and a number of orchestras. They used violins in those days much more... Dance officers than we do now.
What kind of a part, if they played in more or less Dixieland band, in that, say, six or seven piece group, what kind of a part would the violin play?
Always, of course, the lead. Just stick to the lead. You didn't... Oh, all right.
They didn't try to get fancy and run...
Well, yes, we had boys there who were pretty clever with that sort of thing. You mean improvisation? Yes, improvisation. Yeah.
They did that then, too. I wondered if they just stuck to the lead. Did you hear any parades when you were a boy? Can you remember? Of course, the Mardi Gras parades, I guess, you can't miss those.
Oh, my gosh, yes, parades and funerals with bands.
You used the brass band?
And the very last job that I booked before I left there was the carnival parade of that year. I had a band that played for the King's Chariot. That was my last big job before I came to Chicago.
Was that on the street or the carnival ball?
On the street. On the street. Oh, no, we never played any of the ball.
That was in the parade.
That was the parade, yes.
What did you play in the parade? Sax?
No, at that time I was playing baritone horn.
Baritone horn. Mm-hmm. I wondered about the saxophone when you were a boy there, or young, I don't mean by a boy five years old, but I mean up to the...
I didn't start the saxophone until I came here to Stratford Hotel.
Because they used many...
At that time, if you remember the Brown Brothers here in Vaudeville?
Yeah. The six Brown Brothers.

Well, we decided we'd all take up saxophones. And we went over to Conn and bought a whole set of saxophones. And we had one of the men, the only, at that time, the only tenor saxophone player we had among our group, happened to be working with us. And he was our instructor. And we bought these saxophones. We had a baritone. We had a tenor. Two altos. And after a few lessons, we developed a couple of quartets. And during the dinner hour, we used to lay down these regular instruments and then play saxophone quartets, imitating the Brown Brothers. And of course, everybody liked it so well, we just stayed with it.
Did they use the saxophone very much in New Orleans, if you can remember?
No,
Or the big brass bands, do you remember? Or say the lyric band, they wouldn't have used anything.
No, no.
Of course there, but I mean the other bands.
No, the saxophone came into popularity much, much later than that.
I think they say the saxophone was invented by a Frenchman or from Belgium.
By the name of Sax. Aldo. Yes, Adolf Sax.
So you would think that if it were a French...
It's a development from an instrument that was called a sax, but... Oh yes, I remember.

You read my history. I'm wondering, since you remember the old French opera, I know it's hard to think back that many years, too, when you were a boy and went to the French opera, but can you remember anything about the orchestra, how many players, is it a pretty big...

You mean in the orchestra, at the opera? In the pit, yes. Oh my gosh, yes. I don't think, far as I can remember, there were under 50 men in the pit. Regular symphonic outfit. Regular symphonic outfit. Oh yes, yes. It was a monster thing.
Did they have opera about every night? Yes.
Uh-huh. You'd go only to five. And the thing that made it nice for us, that you could go in the gallery for 35 cents. 35? Mm-hmm.
Pretty good.
Yeah.
Opera prices are high.
Yeah, and we heard some very fine, some very fine artists.
Can you remember any famous singers or rich opera?
Of course, I don't know if they would match up with the present day opera singers, but in those days, we thought they were very wonderful.
I always heard too, the New Orleans French Opera was one of the best in the country.
I don't think they have that anymore.
Oh no, they do have some opera at the auditorium now. Maybe...
Yeah, but they're not the original New Orleans opera company. Oh no, that opera house... They don't have their own opera company as they did in those days.
They don't even have the opera house, it's a municipal auditorium. Oh yeah. The opera house burned down in 1919. Oh.
So, uh... That's the old opera house on Bourbon Street. On Bourbon and Tulips.

Yeah. It's a big parking lot. Yeah. Is that so? It's a big parking lot. All the nightclubs are right, started all around in there, nightclubs, and strip joints, you know, for all the strip girls. That's all.
Sometimes I might run down there and look the field of... I haven't been there in. Oh.
I was gonna ask, how long?
I haven't been there now. See, my father died in 22. I haven't been there since.
1922. Oh, do you have any other relatives living there?
Not anymore. What few relatives we have left, they have moved to Seattle. A couple of cousins, retired school teachers, and my sister and brother, they've been here with me. Oh, any number of years.
Your teacher at the French Opera, you say he was the assistant conductor. Assistant conductor there.
Did he play an instrument too, sometimes?
Oh, yes.
He was violinist. Oh, the concertmaster. Oh, yeah.
I know a lot of times the concertmaster is the assistant conductor. Yeah. I didn't know if he just waved to the car.
Oh, he was a wonderful man. I shall always be thankful to him. He was marvelous.
Do you remember hearing any good concert violinists when you were a boy and a student there at that time? Did they give recitals in the French Opera too, or just opera?

Well, we didn't get too many of them, because of course you know what New Orleans was in those days. The only one I can remember very vividly, and it's this old man I told you about, B-Day, that this orchestra sent over there to study. And when he came, he made one trip after he was a grown man and gave one recital.
And you got the hearing.
And I played in the orchestra that was on the program. At that time I had developed enough to play in the orchestra. That played.

Can you tell me some of your favorite musicians that you've heard? I'm not trying to put you on the spot, because I know that you're in your... Well, there's so many. There's so many. I have... I mean some of the old timers maybe that aren't even living now on different instruments that you've liked.

Well, there are a lot of... Among the newcomers that I admire greatly and have all the respect in the world for them on various instruments. There's a young fella I met about four or five years ago. He's originally from Cleveland. He's living in New York now. Violinist by the name of Everett Lee. He's also a very fine composer. He has toured Europe. The last card I had from, he was touring South America, conducting all the various symphonies there. When he first came to New York, it was just when Carmen Jones had started. Leonard Bernstein had the orchestra.
Oh, yes.

Leonard Bernstein was so carried away with his talent that they made him the concert master of that orchestra. And any time Leonard felt that he wanted to take a rest, he let Everett take the orchestra. And after they closed the season in New York and went on the road, he didn't leave New York. He sent Everett Lee with the outfit.
I've been trying my...

Since I met him and heard him and saw him in action, I've been trying to get him a date here in Chicago to Grant Park. I haven't been successful so far. They always have some lame excuse. But the boy has done a grand, grand job.
I was going to ask too about Eddie's South. Is he still playing around here?
Eddie... Eddie's not doing as well as he should with his talent. How's his health?
Did he have TB? You know, it's...
Now his health's fine. You'll never know that he was sick a day. He's as big as a house.
He looks fine.
By the way, he is my pupil.
Oh, is that right?
I don't know.
That's right.
You can be proud of him, I think. But there's something wrong with Eddie's makeup that's holding him back. He, as you know, he has all the talent.
Yes, I thought so too.
Very gifted, very talented. But there's something that's holding him back and it's not his music.
Yeah, it's lucky that he didn't have some health recovery anyway.
No, no, no.
One good thing.
No, because after he came out of the hospital, they put him right to work. But I don't know. He doesn't seem to...

I heard him about four years ago when he was up on the north side. Do you remember Clark Street there? I think there's State Street, about there. State Street, a little place. About state and... I don't know, Division. He played there all winter.
Yeah. He's had a few spots here where he do... He was on Rush Street. I can't think of the name of the place. Oh, yeah. Oh, but he was there possibly for four, six weeks.
Are there any other of your pupils that you can think of now that are famous, or well-known names?

Well, not as much as Eddie, because Eddie was fortunate enough to make this European tour, which really had much to do with his success, because he was a huge success at that time. But I have had quite a bit of success with most of the pupils I had at that time. But they didn't go in for concert work. They did most orchestra work. It was Jimmy Bell. And when they had the orchestra at the Regal Theatre, we had a couple of boys in there. I can't think of their names now. To get back to some of the other instruments, like on trumpet...
...and the other instruments, like on trumpet...

You of course heard a lot of King Oliver and Freddie Keppard, and of course Louis Armstrong, all of those New Orleans trumpet players, so many great ones that I don't know which one you can pick. Oh yes, there are a lot of
new fellas now, I don't know these boys only by reputation who are, the boys who are with Basie and Duke, oh those boys are just
wonderful, marvelous. Yeah they have a lot of technique and range, but I still don't think they have quite a tone. Oh my yeah, but it brings us back to what we were
speaking in the beginning, those boys have had fine training, fine schooling.
Can you remember much about the Oliver band when they were here? Well they were pretty much
on the same order of the average Dixieland outfit, they were all very good, but I wouldn't say nothing too extraordinary.

I wondered about their reception, of course the people like myself are more or less a fanatic on the New Orleans style of music, and to me they were so wonderful, just to hear them on the record, what's left. And I wasn't here in those days to hear them, but did they go over unusually well? I mean, did they have the general public or was it just the

certainly the cafe? No, no, no, not at that time. The public hadn't taken to the to the Dixieland idea of music. Of course the music lovers who like that type of thing, they went for it. But not as popular as it is now. You take now, you take these young colleges, these young boys who are in colleges now, my gosh, they go all out for that type of thing. And even having these fellas lecture in these colleges. Duke, Duke has lectured at Yale, at Harvard, all these fine institutions. Look what's happening at Ravinia. Lionel Hampton is on the bill there. Earl Garner is on the bill there. Those things were unheard of years ago.
That's right. But I wondered if the general public, or if it was just the small group, I know it wasn't just the South Side.
It's the general public if you judge from the attendance.

I mean, in the Oliver days, back in the 1920s, say when Keppert and Oliver and Emmanuel Perez and all of those people played here. If it was just a small group that followed them, or if it was a lot of the whole Chicago public that would come to dance to their music. For instance, say at Royal Garden, was that mostly...
Royal Garden? That was just another nightclub.
Just another nightclub.
Just another nightclub.
Was that mostly for whites or the colored crowd? Oh, no, that was for everybody. Everybody, but... Yeah. People from all over Chicago would go there.
Oh, yeah, sure, sure.
So it wasn't just restricted like a neighborhood place. No, no, no.
Oh, no, no, no, no.

Uh-oh. The whole city would go there then at times. Mm-hmm. Of course, in those days they didn't have much radio, naturally no television, so they didn't get a chance to become nationally known. That's it.
That's another thing. See, that's an advantage that the present day outfit has now. The radio and TV, we didn't have that even in my days. No.
See, we never had that.
Of course, we had good fortune of having a man who was a wonderful promoter, Patty Harmon.
Oh, yes, I must have asked about that.
And he did all the publicizing of our outfit. In fact, he was the making of the outfit because we had the orchestra pictures all over the L station.
I took some pictures of that 20 years ago.
Yeah, sure.
The old Harmon's Greenland out on Palina.
That's right.
And you were in the back.
Then we'd go from one job to the other because he was running the pier. At that time it was called a municipal pier.
Is that where the Navy pier is?
That's where the Navy pier is now. At that time he had the contract with the city to run it. We'd go from Dreamland on Sunday before Labor Day and move over to the pier on Labor Day.
Stay there in the winter then?
Stay there all winter.

That's good. See if there's any more questions here about these early days. It's mostly the early days that we're asking about because a lot of the later things we could read in the newspapers and the magazines and downbeat. Yeah. Back before they had a downbeat for instance.

Well, I went in with Patty with five pieces. That's when the craze of Dixonland music had just begun to hit Chicago. And I went to see him and ask him if he'd give me a chance with this outfit. At that time he had an 18 piece white orchestra. Frank Cavallo had the orchestra there. And he kind of hesitated for a minute because he didn't know how people would go for it. And I was fortunate enough to sell him on the idea of giving it a trial, which he agreed to do. Well, we went in there with the understanding that if the thing didn't go over and if the authorities didn't, because there was no such thing in any ballroom in Chicago prior to this time. He said, now, there was a Mrs. Bimford who was a welfare worker. He said, now, she comes in here all the time and if she doesn't go for this type of thing, she says, I'll have to let you go. I said, it's perfectly all right. I'm willing to take my chances. Well, we went in there as a trial. About the second week, she came in there and began to say that our type of music was a little too boisterous for the young people. Too rough.
Rough. Who was in the band, do you remember?
Huh?
The trumpet player, for instance.

We had Joe, the same boy. See, I didn't change very much. You didn't change? No, no, no. Those boys stayed with me right on through. The clarinet, do you remember? I was playing Clown Insect for myself. Oh, you were playing Clown Insect for yourself. Yeah. And after the second week, he said, well, I'm afraid we're going to have to dismiss you because she's complaining too much. I said, well, that was the agreement, it's all right. Well, we were there just long enough to have won over the young dancers, all of the young people. At that time, they were mostly young Jewish people, Italians, from over in that area. And they all went for our type of music. And they started complaining about when you're going to get this band back, when you're going to get this band back, when you're going to get this band back. So after about a month, here comes a telephone call. He said, you better come over here and let me have a talk. I said, I'll go back over there and have a talk on it. He said, well, we're going to make another stab at it and see what happens. Well, it was funny. He said, I'm going to let you see who Miss Bimford is. And whenever you see her come in that door, regardless of which you play, you start playing a waltz. And I followed instructions. And finally, we see her come in and she'd sit around there, maybe sometimes a half hour, maybe an hour. We didn't play anything but the sweetest type of foxtrot, you know. Then we finally won her over. See, well, that was the story. After we did that, well, there was no more trouble. In the meantime, why, Paddy decided that he wanted to increase the band and we kept on adding first one and then we had another until we had, from five, we had increased the orchestra to 15 pieces.
Was the bandstand right at that corner, like there's Van Buren and the...
No, the bandstand was, the bandstand was about the center of the hall. If you remember, that hall was a whole block long.
But right inside, remember, then the elevator went right over that one corner.

No, at that corner there was where the bar was on one side and the office was on the opposite side. But the bandstand was way up about the center and in the later days, it was in the center of the floor. Right in the very center, the people used to dance around us.
Yeah, I remember now seeing a picture with Jimmy Lee sitting on the... That's right. ...and that's when Cook was there.
We had a picture there with Charlie Cook because Charlie Cook followed me in there. I've seen that picture. Well, that was put right in the center of the ballroom.
Yeah, that's what it does look like, that one I think. Yeah. I guess I remember. Well, that's just a great place, isn't it?
Yeah, we spent so many very happy hours there.

Well, before we stop, I don't want to keep you for another two or three minutes, but since there are none of the TOs left to speak for themselves and give us any of their history, if there's anything else you can think of, I don't like to keep harping on them, but I'd love one more in question. I'd love one more in final chance. Anything about, it was Louis Keough was your teacher. Don't worry about him. That's all, you won't make any. Can you remember, did he speak much English or did he speak much in Keough? Oh, yes, oh, yes, oh, yes, sure. Oh, yes, sure. Oh, yes, sure. Or was it Spanish if he came from Mexico?
They spoke Spanish, but they developed the English and French. Oh, yes, you'd never know. You'd never know that they weren't originally all these fellas.
Because I have heard sometimes people will imitate their talk a little bit, they'll use sort of the French accent.
Yeah, but they didn't even have the Spanish accent. They didn't even have that? No. But when you saw them, you know you were looking at a Mexican. They had, you know, they're a certain type.
I've never even seen a good picture of them. No? Lorenzo Jr., I've seen him. He had sort of long, black, wavy hair. Uh-huh. A real good-looking fellow. A great big fellow.
Oh, yeah, they both were. But how were they? And I can't, I don't know that I've ever seen a picture of the old man.
I don't think I have.
Neither one, Lorenzo Narlo.
Were they fairly tall? Oh, I know. Somebody told me that Joe Oliver's the widow, Stella Oliver has one in New Orleans. I haven't had her. Is that so? So we'll get to see her, maybe she'll have one.
Uh-huh.
I don't know which one.
Are you on your way there from here?

I just came up from there. I'll be there, I'll only be here a week and I'll go back. I see. So I'll get to see her within a month or two now. And she had a picture of one of the Teos, either Louie or Lorenzo. You knew them both, I guess, then, fairly well, did you?
Oh, oh, yes, I should say, very well.
Your teacher was Louie. Yeah. Louie Teos. He's the one I think they usually call Papa Teos.
Yeah, that's right. That's right. Louie's the one we used to call Papa Teos. Yeah.

And the other was Lorenzo Sr., they call him now. And the Junior is the one that was with P. Rowland's band, went to New York, made Rutgers. Yeah. The others never made Rutgers. Well, unless there's something else you can think of about the Teos, I think we can-
Well, I think we've about covered everything I can think of so far as they are concerned,
you know? Yes. Unless there's something else you want to tell about either your life or your early days in New Orleans? Oh, I can't think of it.
I guess I've about covered everything I can think of now. I think we've covered everything pretty good, and I thought there might be something you
could think of, but if not, I will. I want to thank you again for the-
Well, that's all right.
Thank you, it's been a pleasure to talk to you and have your voice now on record. So we're going to just turn it off. Turn it off. Turn it off. Thank you.

segments.title: Opening: name and birth date in New Orleans
segments.summary: Elgar gives his birth date, June 13, 1879, and full name.

segments.title: Starting violin at six with a French opera teacher
segments.summary: His family was not musical; he began violin at six with the assistant conductor of the French opera, studying six years.

segments.title: Hearing French opera as a boy in Frenchtown
segments.summary: Opera was his first music; his parents took him to the opera and his teacher got him into rehearsals.

segments.title: Turning to clarinet with the Tio brothers
segments.summary: He moved to popular music after clarinet study with Louis Tio, a Mexican-born brother of Lorenzo; Tio pupils like Baquet, McCurdy, Noone and Nicholas.

segments.title: The Tio school and its pupils; Louis traveled, Lorenzo taught
segments.summary: Buster Bailey also came from that school; Lorenzo mostly taught at home while Louis toured with minstrel shows.

segments.title: Mexican band at the 1885 Cotton Exposition and the Garde Republicaine
segments.summary: The huge Mexican symphonic band in New Orleans, and the French Garde Republicaine heard in World War I at the pier.

segments.title: Brass bands and first road trip with a circus band
segments.summary: He toured with an outfit from St. Louis, was stranded, led a circus orchestra with trumpeter P.G. Lowry, and went to New York.

segments.title: Catholic church and leaving for Chicago in 1902
segments.summary: He is a lifelong Catholic and left New Orleans in November 1902.

segments.title: Arriving in Chicago and joining Local 208
segments.summary: He joined Local 208 soon after its charter, discusses past presidents, serves as vice president and leads a concert orchestra for the Music Performance Trust Fund.

segments.title: Early schooling: Nelson Academy and Southern University
segments.summary: He attended a private school next door to his birthplace, as his father rejected public schools.

segments.title: Chicago studies and the Club Lyri with Louis Tio conducting
segments.summary: He studied at Marquette, Kimball Hall and the YMCA college, and learned conducting from Louis Tio in the nonprofit Club Lyri orchestra.

segments.title: Classical training versus the dance field
segments.summary: The Tio pupils went to dance music; Elgar says Dixieland demands real technique and trained musicians.

segments.title: First Dixieland in Chicago: Bill Johnson and the Ansonia
segments.summary: Bill Johnson's band came first; Elgar brought Perez, Tio and Cottrell from New Orleans to the Ansonia for Mike Fritzel.

segments.title: Mike Fritzel's later restaurant
segments.summary: Brief talk about Mike Fritzel's death and the restaurant bearing his name.

segments.title: New Orleans musicians versus young players today
segments.summary: He says New Orleans men had better training than today's riff players, and notes young Black musicians now entering symphonies.

segments.title: Richard Davis, Fosbender and Elgar's violin
segments.summary: Richard Davis studied under Fosbender; Elgar has lost hearing in one ear and describes his violin by a German maker.

segments.title: Elgar's Peerless Orchestra records and personnel
segments.summary: He dislikes the poorly rehearsed Vocalion and Brunswick records; he lists Darnell Howard, Joe Sudler, Harry Swift, Logan Thomas and others.

segments.title: Identifying musicians in band photographs
segments.summary: Elgar names men in photographs, including Omer Simeon, Harry Beasley, Will Washington, Bill Buford and Ernest Smith.

segments.title: Milwaukee roof garden, Eagles Ballroom and the Savoy
segments.summary: The band spent years at the Wisconsin Roof Garden and Eagles Ballroom in Milwaukee, the Stratford Hotel, then opened the Savoy in Chicago.

segments.title: New Orleans players in the band; Freddie Keppard
segments.summary: He wanted Zutty Singleton but Louis Armstrong was forming his own band; Freddie Keppard played with him.

segments.title: Dance music and halls in New Orleans
segments.summary: He played with Fields and Planchet for club dances, at halls like Francs Amis.

segments.title: Violin in New Orleans dance bands
segments.summary: Violins played lead in dance orchestras, with clarinet central in Dixieland groups; some improvised.

segments.title: Carnival parade job before leaving, on baritone horn
segments.summary: His last big New Orleans job was a band for the King's Chariot in the carnival parade.

segments.title: Taking up saxophone in Chicago; saxophone in New Orleans
segments.summary: Inspired by the Six Brown Brothers, his group bought saxophones at the Stratford Hotel; saxophone was uncommon in New Orleans.

segments.title: The French Opera House: orchestra, prices and fate
segments.summary: The pit held about 50 men, the gallery cost 35 cents, and the building burned in 1919.

segments.title: Family, his teacher and a concert violinist
segments.summary: His father died in 1922, relatives have moved away, and he recalls his teacher and one violin recital.

segments.title: Admired musicians: violinist Everett Lee
segments.summary: He praises Everett Lee, who conducted for Carmen Jones, and has tried to get him a Grant Park date.

segments.title: Pupil Eddie South and other students
segments.summary: Eddie South was his pupil, talented but held back; other pupils worked in orchestras.

segments.title: Oliver band reception and changing audiences for jazz
segments.summary: Oliver's band was good but not extraordinary; the public then was not yet taken with Dixieland, unlike now.

segments.title: Royal Garden audience and lack of radio
segments.summary: Royal Garden was an ordinary nightclub for everyone; radio and television did not exist then.

segments.title: Promoter Paddy Harmon, Dreamland and the municipal pier
segments.summary: Harmon publicized the band and ran Dreamland and the pier, where the band moved after Labor Day.

segments.title: Introducing Dixieland at Harmon's ballroom and winning over the welfare worker
segments.summary: Elgar's five-piece band went on trial against Mrs. Bimford's objections, won over the young dancers, and grew to fifteen.

segments.title: The Tio brothers: language, looks and photographs
segments.summary: Last questions about Louis and Lorenzo Tio: they spoke Spanish, English and French, and no photographs are known.

segments.title: Closing remarks and thanks
segments.summary: Nothing more to add; the interviewer thanks him and ends the recording.
